query: The Co-free FeNiCrMn system was selected to reduce cost while retaining the mechanical performance of equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi; prior work reported comparable or better mechanical properties after excluding Co. Research on FeNiCrMn has mainly addressed corrosion, while studies of related high- and medium-entropy alloys examined dynamic responses under tension or compression, different temperatures and strain rates, compositional changes, and the presence of cracks or voids. Those studies established that dynamic properties are sensitive to loading regime and material condition, but their different chemistries and defect states do not identify what governs FeNiCrMn. Under the constraints of retaining the Co-free composition and its strength–ductility balance, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis explains the dynamic behavior of solidified FeNiCrMn across temperature and strain-rate regimes? Define a controlled study capable of testing the hypothesis, its applicable boundaries, the prior findings that support it, and a result that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: The dynamic mechanical response of as‐solidified, Co‐free FeNiCrMn is controlled by a transition in the operative plasticity mechanism—from dislocation glide at higher temperatures (and/or low strain rates) to enhanced deformation twinning at lower temperatures (and/or high strain rates)—which drives the observed strain rate sensitivity and strength–ductility balance.
generation.material_initial_state: As‐solidified, compositionally fixed FeNiCrMn alloy processed to maintain an optimal strength–ductility balance.
generation.intervention: Systematically vary the testing temperature and strain rate during tensile/compression and split‐Hopkinson pressure bar experiments while maintaining a constant microstructure.
generation.conditions: Test conditions spanning a broad temperature range (e.g., cryogenic around 77 K up to elevated temperatures near 1073 K) and from quasi‐static strain rates (~10⁻³ s⁻¹) to high dynamic strain rates (≥10³ s⁻¹), ensuring that only temperature and strain rate are varied.
generation.structural_mediator: The emergence and/or increase in twin boundary density relative to dislocation structures in the microstructure (observable by TEM) as loading conditions move into the low-temperature/high strain-rate regime.
generation.mechanism: At higher temperatures and lower strain rates, plasticity is primarily accommodated by dislocation glide. As temperature decreases and/or strain rate increases, the material progressively activates deformation twinning, which provides extra barriers to dislocation motion and increases strain hardening, thereby reinforcing the strength–ductility balance.
generation.predicted_outcome: Under low-temperature and high strain-rate conditions, the yield strength will increase along with a higher density of deformation twins (as compared to conditions favoring dislocation glide), resulting in a measurable shift in deformation mechanisms observed via TEM and correlated with increased strain rate sensitivity.
generation.baseline: All tests are performed on the same as‐solidified FeNiCrMn alloy with a constant microstructure, ensuring that only the loading conditions (temperature and strain rate) dictate the deformation mechanism.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis applies within the tested ranges (approximately 77 K to 1073 K and strain rates from quasi‐static to high dynamic regimes). Outside these regimes, other effects (e.g., adiabatic shear banding or oxidation at very high temperatures) may dominate.
generation.uncertainty: The precise temperature or strain rate at which the transition becomes dominant is not yet defined; additionally, potential minor influences from residual impurities or slight microstructural variations are uncertain.

falsification_experiment.design: Conduct a matrix of dynamic mechanical tests (both tensile and compression), systematically varying temperature (e.g., 77 K, 300 K, 673 K, 1073 K) and strain rate (e.g., ~10⁻³ s⁻¹, 10³ s⁻¹, 10⁵ s⁻¹) on identically prepared, as‐solidified FeNiCrMn specimens. Use in situ or detailed ex situ TEM to quantify the evolution of dislocation densities and twin boundaries.
measurements: Yield strength and strain rate sensitivity
Quantitative TEM analysis of dislocation structures and twin boundary fractions
Fractography to correlate failure mechanisms with deformation modes
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the microstructural analysis shows no significant increase in deformation twinning (i.e., twin boundary density remains constant relative to dislocation density) across the range of low-temperature/high strain rate tests, or if the mechanical data (yield strength and strain rate sensitivity) do not correlate with a shift in the dominant deformation mechanism, then the hypothesis is falsified.

occupying_moves.technique: dynamic mechanical testing (e.g., split‐Hopkinson pressure bar) combined with microstructural characterization
occupying_moves.conditions: using as-solidified, compositionally fixed FeNiCrMn samples processed to maintain the strength–ductility balance, tested over a broad temperature range (cryogenic to elevated) and varying strain rates to isolate the intrinsic mechanism

occupying_moves.technique: systematic dynamic tensile/compression testing along with in situ or ex situ transmission electron microscopy (TEM) to monitor deformation mechanisms
occupying_moves.conditions: on Co-free, as-solidified FeNiCrMn specimens with standardized microstructures, covering regimes from low to high strain rates and from low (cryogenic) to high temperatures to resolve whether a transition from dislocation glide to deformation twinning (or other mechanism) governs the dynamic response

chosen.technique: dynamic mechanical testing (e.g., split‐Hopkinson pressure bar and tensile/compression tests) paired with microstructural analysis (TEM)
chosen.conditions: on Co-free, as-solidified FeNiCrMn alloys that preserve the strength–ductility balance, tested systematically across a range of temperatures (from cryogenic to high temperature) and strain rates to capture the potential transition between dislocation-mediated plasticity and deformation twinning
chosen.why: This move directly addresses the open question by isolating the effect of temperature and strain-rate on the dynamic behavior while keeping the composition and resulting microstructure constant. It tests the mechanistic hypothesis that the dynamic performance arises from a transition or interplay between deformation mechanisms (e.g., dislocation glide versus twinning) triggered by the loading conditions—a hypothesis that is both testable and falsifiable using standard, controlled-variable experiments in the field.
